title: Minimal-footprint edge appliance design for air-gapped private deployments
author: Maya Chen
body:
Summary

Purpose: Provide a prescriptive, minimal-footprint edge appliance design and deployment runbook for air-gapped/private Redwood Inference deployments where constrained rack space, limited power, and strict egress controls are required. This document complements the broader airgap packaging guidance by focusing on compact appliance form factors, deterministic telemetry, and safe field upgrade/rollback for sites with limited physical access.

Goals

- Define a hardware and software baseline for a single-unit edge appliance capable of serving small private-tenancy inference workloads (single-tenant or up to 2 small tenants).
- Specify secure packaging, transit, and on-site installation procedures minimizing human error during field installs.
- Provide day-2 operational procedures: health checks, telemetry collection (sampling), emergency rollback, and secure image updates for airgapped environments.

Scope

- Applies to on-premises, air-gapped/private deployments where customers/operators require a single-rack or single-unit appliance (approx. 1U/2U) for edge inference. Not intended for large multi-rack dedicated deployments.
- Assumes customer or partner handles physical transport; this document focuses on appliance configuration, acceptance, and operator procedures.

High-level architecture

The appliance is a self-contained inference node running the Redwood Private runtime with a lightweight control agent. Key components:

- Base OS: Hardened Linux (Ubuntu LTS minimal or Rocky 9 minimal) with kernel lockdown and FIPS-compatible crypto libs.
- Runtime: Redwood inference container runtime (signed images), local control agent that communicates with a customer-managed control plane when permitted.
- Storage: Encrypted NVMe for model artifacts and KV cache, with a small encrypted persistent partition for logs/telemetry buffer.
- Networking: Single management NIC (redundant if chassis allows) and single inference NIC. All egress blocked by default; allowed destinations only via customer-provided proxy or physical sneakernet for images.

Hardware baseline (minimum recommended)

| Component | Minimum | Preferred | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| CPU | 8 cores (Xeon D / AMD EPYC embedded class) | 16 cores | Handle control-plane tasks and light pre/post processing |
| GPU | 1x 80GB-class A100/RTX 6000 Ada | 1x H800 or 2x smaller accelerators | Choice depends on inference model size; provide quantized profile if smaller GPU used |
| Memory | 256 GB DDR4 | 512 GB | Host + model KV cache headroom |
| Local storage | 1 x 2TB NVMe (encrypted) | 2 x 2TB NVMe (RAID1) | RAID1 preferred for resilience |
| TPM | Discrete TPM 2.0 | - | Required for image attestation |
| Power | Single 400W PSU | Redundant PSUs if chassis supports | Low-power PSU to fit constrained sites |

Network and firewall requirements (operator-visible)

| Interface | Direction | Port(s) | Purpose |
|---|---|---:|---|
| mgmt0 | outbound (to on-prem proxy) | 443, 853 (DNS over TLS) | Image fetch and attestation when allowed |
| infer0 | inbound (customer network) | Variable (gRPC/HTTP endpoints) | Application traffic to model endpoints |
| node-agent | outbound (to ops VPN) | 22/443 | Secure operator SSH/agent tunnel (customer-controlled) |

By default, appliance egress is disabled. Operators must provide an allowlist for the exact FQDNs/IPs and present the appliance certificate for approval.

Packaging and transit checklist

1) Image sealing and signing
   - Build images in CI with image signing using the company KMS.
   - Include an immutable manifest with image checksum and build-id.
   - Seal image artifacts in a tamper-evident archive (e.g., signed tar + SHA256).
2) Hardware pre-configuration
   - Provision TPM with vendor keys and inject device serial into manifest.
   - Preload encrypted provisioning bundle onto a sealed USB and label with site identifier.
3) Physical packaging
   - Use anti-static, shock-absorbing inserts and numbered tamper seals.
   - Include manifest, acceptance checklist, and emergency recovery USB in sealed envelope.

On-site installation procedure (operator-facing, numbered)

1. Verify tamper seals and physical manifest match the order (serials, model). If mismatch, stop and escalate to field-ops.
2. Racked power: connect PSU(s) to specified PDUs (note power budget).
3. Connect management NIC to customer-managed isolated management VLAN. Block general egress on the port (apply MAC/IP lock if available).
4. Boot device once; watch for 'firstboot' console messages. Firstboot performs local KMS injection and disk unlock using sealed provisioning bundle.
5. Run acceptance tests (see Acceptance checklist below). Record and sign results in the attached acceptance form.

Acceptance criteria (operator checklist)

- Appliance boots to login prompt within 90 seconds of first OS init.
- TPM attestation passes and device manifest matches signed image manifest.
- Local inference health endpoint (HTTP /health) returns OK and reports model artifact checksum.
- NVMe SMART status: no pre-failure indicators.
- Telemetry buffer initialized and encrypted.
- Operator can establish a mutually authenticated tunnel to the agent port (if customer permits).

Telemetry and health (day-2 guidance)

Constraints: Air-gapped sites cannot stream continuous telemetry. We recommend the following hybrid approach:

- Local high-resolution capture: collect CPU/GPU metrics, per-request latencies, and resource utilization at 1s - 10s resolution locally for 72 hours in a ring buffer (encrypted).
- Summarized telemetry snapshots: periodic compact digests (hourly) with aggregated metrics and anomaly markers stored locally.
- Operator-triggered offload: site operator exports the encrypted snapshot bundle via secure USB for upload to Redwood support in cases of degraded health.

Telemetry retention policy (on-appliance):

- High-res ring buffer: 72 hours default (configurable).
- Summarized snapshots: 30 days (rolling).

Upgrade and rollback strategy (airgapped safe flow)

Principles: upgrades must be atomic, signed, and reversible without external egress. Use phased local staging and checksum verification.

Standard offline upgrade flow (numbered):

1. Operator transfers signed image bundle to appliance via sealed USB.
2. Appliance verifies signature with embedded vendor public key and checks manifest.
3. Appliance creates a read-only snapshot of current model artifacts and runtime configuration (immutable copy).
4. Appliance mounts staging overlay and performs dry-run with a small synthetic request set to validate runtime.
4a. If dry-run fails, automated rollback to snapshot is triggered and operator alerted.
5. On successful dry-run, appliance switches symlink to new runtime artifacts and reboots services.
6. Post-upgrade smoke tests run for 15 minutes; if 5xx rate exceeds 1% or latency p50 doubles, automatic rollback kicks in.

Rollback playbook (emergency)

- Trigger: sustained 5xx > 1% over 15m or p50 latency > 2x baseline for 10 minutes.
- Steps: initiate local rollback command; if command fails, reboot into recovery partition (read-only snapshot). If hardware-level fault suspected, escalate to field replacement.

Security controls and attestations

- All runtime images must be signed and verified against the embedded vendor key prior to execution.
- Disk encryption: LUKS2 with TPM-bound keys. Keys are unlocked only during firstboot using sealed provisioning bundle.
- SSH: disabled by default; agent-based mutual TLS for operator tunnels only.
- Audit: critical actions (upgrade, key rotation, manifest verification) appended to an append-only audit log located on the encrypted partition.

Day-2 operational playbook (quick reference)

1. Routine weekly: verify audit log rotation, check NVMe SMART, snapshot of summarized telemetry to removable media.
2. Monthly: run a full acceptance checklist and validate image checksums against the sealed manifest.
3. Incident: collect encrypted snapshot, notify Redwood support channel, and if allowed provide sealed USB for full forensic upload.

Performance and SLO guidance

- Target p50 latency: <= 50ms for small text generation models on the preferred hardware baseline.
- Error budget: <= 0.5% 5xx across rolling 7-day window for single-tenant appliances.
- Throughput guidance: 10–20 concurrent small requests for 80GB-class GPUs; scale guidance included in capacity annex.

Ownership and escalation

- Initial field operator: partner or customer engineering team (document contact in on-site manifest).
- Redwood private deploy officer: Maya Chen (owner) — ops@redwood.ai on internal address. Escalation policy: P1 -> oncall infra -> engineering runtime -> security if image integrity issues.

Appendix A — Acceptance test CLI snippets

- Verify health endpoint: curl -fsS --unix-socket /var/run/redwood.sock http://localhost/health
- Verify image manifest: /usr/local/bin/hash-verify /opt/artifacts/manifest.json

Appendix B — Compact capacity annex (guidance, not absolute)

- Small: 1x 80GB GPU, 256 GB RAM — supports models up to ~7B dense with quantization profiles.
- Medium: 1x H800, 512 GB RAM — supports ~13B–30B models with optimized kernels.
- Recommend conservative headroom: reserve 20% GPU memory for KV cache and orchestration overhead.

References

- See also: airgap-packaging-and-day2-hardening-2026 (packaging baseline)
- Edge gateway and airgapped bridge architecture reference (network bridge patterns)
